Comments: Value=0. Searched for: Burundi payment consumer protection law; e-money/mobile money consumer protection regulation; dispute resolution requirements by BRB/ARCT. Did not find an authoritative, specific payments consumer protection framework text in accessible sources used for scoring.

revision_notes: Light-check search (per fast-path routing) surfaced a clearly authoritative primary source, so the row was moved to the full path. The Banque de la République du Burundi (BRB) publishes Règlement N°001/2019 relatif à la protection des consommateurs des produits et services financiers, enforced via a sanctions matrix (Circulaire N°01/2020, revised by Circulaire N°006/SP/2024) that explicitly covers digital/electronic financial services, disclosure, complaints handling and account management. This is a dedicated, government-published, payment-specific consumer protection framework, fetched and read directly from brb.bi. Value code changed from 0 (Unknown) to 3 (Yes - comprehensive).
revised_comments: The Bank of the Republic of Burundi (BRB) has enacted Règlement N°001/2019 relatif à la protection des consommateurs des produits et services financiers, a dedicated consumer protection regulation covering digital financial services, disclosure requirements, complaints handling, account opening/closure and marketing conduct. Compliance is enforced through a sanctions matrix (Circulaire N°01/2020, revised by Circulaire N°006/SP/2024) that specifically addresses breaches involving digital financial services and data confidentiality. This constitutes a comprehensive, payment-specific consumer protection framework overseen by the central bank.

Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: Value=0. Searched for: Burundi data breach notification requirement; cybersecurity law breach notification; CERT incident reporting obligations. Found references to cybercrime/cybersecurity discussions but no credible, explicit legal requirement for mandatory vs discretionary breach notification in sources reviewed.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light-check search surfaced conflicting claims, so the row was moved to the full path. DLA Piper's Data Protection Laws of the World reference (authoritative, last updated January 2024, fetched and read directly) states explicitly that 'there are no breach notification requirements in Burundi', noting the country has no dedicated data protection law - only sector-specific confidentiality obligations (banking secrecy under the 2017 Banking Act art.133, healthcare confidentiality, telecommunications privacy rules, and the 2022 Law on Cybercriminality's provisions on personal data, which impose sanctions for unauthorised access but no notification duty). A secondary blog source (generisonline.com) claimed a mandatory 72-hour notification requirement under a 'Law on Personal Data Protection' and a 'CNIL' authority, but cited no specific statute number/year and is inconsistent with the DLA Piper primary legal reference and with the absence of any Burundian data protection authority found elsewhere; this source was discounted as unreliable. Value code changed from 0 (Unknown) to 1 (No mandatory requirement identified).
revised_comments: Burundi has no dedicated data protection law and no general mandatory data breach notification requirement applicable to payment service providers. Confidentiality obligations exist only in sector-specific legislation - banking secrecy under the 2017 Banking Act, healthcare confidentiality rules, telecommunications privacy regulations, and the 2022 Law on the Prevention and Repression of Cybercriminality's provisions on unauthorised access to personal data - none of which impose a duty on providers to notify users, regulators or a data protection authority following a breach.

revision_notes: Light-check search surfaced an authoritative disability-ICT source, so the row was moved to the full path. The G3ict Digital Accessibility Rights Evaluation (DARE) Index (fetched and read directly) scores Burundi 15/100 overall and records explicit 'No policy' (0/5) ratings across every ICT accessibility domain assessed, including mobile telephony and e-government/digital services for all. A GSMA/Concern Worldwide field study of mobile-money-enabled cash assistance in Burundi corroborates the absence of built-in accessibility accommodations, describing recipients with disabilities facing unaddressed practical barriers (e.g. distance to cash-out points) rather than any adaptive design in the payment system itself. No evidence of assistive-technology support, accessible USSD/app design, or disability-specific payment provisions was found. Value code changed from 0 (Unknown) to 1 (No).
revised_comments: No evidence was found of digital payment systems or access points in Burundi (apps, USSD, agent networks) being designed to accommodate persons with disabilities. The G3ict Digital Accessibility Rights Evaluation (DARE) Index records an absence of ICT accessibility policy across all assessed domains, including mobile telephony and e-government/digital services. Field research on mobile-money-enabled cash assistance in Burundi documents unaddressed practical barriers for recipients with disabilities, such as distance to cash-out points, rather than any accessibility accommodation built into the payment platforms themselves.
